body: Respecting yourself can feel unfamiliar, even a little uncomfortable at first. Over roughly ninety days, these notes will help you keep your word to yourself, speak to yourself kindly and expect decent treatment.
For now, simply listen to the voice in your head when something goes wrong. What tone does it take with you? There is nothing to fix yet.
Most of us learned how to talk to ourselves from the people around us when we were small. That habit was absorbed, not chosen, so it can be relearned.
Spot one small promise you made to yourself recently and quietly dropped. Just name it, without any scolding.
Plenty of people are endlessly patient with friends and harsh with themselves. If that sounds familiar, you are in very good company.
Pay attention to the moments you apologise when nothing is actually your fault. Count them if you like, and leave it there.
Self-respect is not arrogance. It is the quiet belief that your needs count as much as anyone else's, no more and no less.
Where in your week do you feel slightly diminished after spending time with someone? Make a mental note of the place, the person or the conversation.
You might find that old patterns get louder when you start paying attention to them. That is a sign of awareness growing, not of failure.
Think of someone you admire for how they carry themselves. What do they do, or refuse to do, that shows they value themselves?
When you catch an unkind phrase in your inner monologue, try asking whether you would ever say it to a colleague. The answer tends to be revealing.
Observe how often you put your own plans last on the list. Awareness of the pattern is the whole task for the moment.
Respect for yourself is built in the same way trust is built with anyone else: through small promises, reliably kept.
Pick one tiny commitment for tomorrow, something you are almost certain to manage, like drinking a glass of water when you wake. Then do it.
Did you keep yesterday's small promise? If yes, let yourself register that. If not, shrink it until it is truly easy and try again.
Your inner critic usually believes it is protecting you. You can thank it for trying and still choose a gentler way of speaking.
Try swapping one harsh word you use about yourself for a neutral one. Lazy might become tired; stupid might become rushed.
Making promises to yourself that are too big sets you up to break them. Smaller, kept commitments do far more for your confidence.
Write down three things you did this week that were genuinely decent, however ordinary. Read the list back slowly.
If someone treated you poorly recently and you laughed it off, revisit it in your mind. How would you have liked to respond?
Expecting decent treatment is not the same as demanding perfection from others. It simply means noticing when the line has been crossed.
Choose one meal this week to eat sitting down, without rushing, as if you were a guest worth looking after.
Next time you make a mistake, try saying to yourself, That was a mistake, and I am still all right. Notice what changes in your body.
Respecting your time is a form of self-respect. Look at tomorrow's plans and ask which of them you agreed to out of guilt alone.
It is fine to keep a promise to yourself imperfectly. Going for a ten-minute walk instead of the planned thirty still counts as keeping faith.
When a friend praises you, experiment with simply saying thank you, without batting it away or explaining why they are wrong.
Your body hears how you talk about it. Pick one part of yourself you usually criticise and say one fair, kind sentence about it instead.
Consider the difference between being liked and being respected. Which one have you been chasing, and at what cost?
Set a small boundary somewhere low-stakes, such as letting a call go to voicemail when you are resting. Observe the guilt, and let it pass.
Guilt after saying no is often just the feeling of an old habit being broken. It fades with practice, the way stiffness fades with stretching.
Ask yourself what a respectful morning would look like for you. Then borrow one element of it for tomorrow.
Halfway through the first month, you might already be catching the critic sooner. That earlier noticing is real progress.
When things are hard, try addressing yourself by your own name in your head, as a coach might. That small distance often softens the tone.
You are allowed to change your mind about a commitment that no longer serves you. Releasing it honestly is kinder than dragging it along.
Look at the people who get your best energy. Are you among them? Find one way to include yourself this week.
When someone interrupts you, try finishing your sentence calmly. A short pause and a steady voice often say enough.
Self-respect grows quietly, through dull, unglamorous repetition. Keeping a promise about bedtime is as valuable as any grand gesture.
Write yourself a short note as you would to a friend going through what you are going through. Keep it somewhere you will see it.
If you notice you are tolerating something that bothers you, ask yourself what you would advise a friend in the same position.
Treat a small task you have been avoiding as a promise worth keeping. Finishing it is a message to yourself that your intentions matter.
Being kind to yourself does not mean letting yourself off every hook. It means holding yourself to account without contempt.
Choose one thing you own that is worn out and annoys you daily. Replacing or mending it is a small way of saying you deserve things that work.
Spend ten minutes doing something purely because you enjoy it. Pleasure is not a reward you must earn first.
When you feel the urge to over-explain a decision, try a shorter version. A clear reason is enough; a long defence is optional.
Halfway through these ninety days, take stock. Which promise to yourself has become easiest to keep, and what made it stick?
People tend to treat us partly according to what we accept. Raising your standards gently can shift how others behave around you.
Try making one request this week without softening it with a joke or an apology. Simply ask, and wait for the answer.
Reflect on a time you stood up for yourself, however small. Remember how it felt afterwards, rather than in the moment.
Some relationships may feel strained as you begin asking for more respect. That tension is information, not proof you are wrong.
Pick a recurring negative thought about yourself and test it like a scientist. What evidence supports it, and what contradicts it?
Rest is not something you have to justify. Take a proper break today and resist the pull to fill it with chores.
Saying I need a moment to think about that is a perfectly respectable answer. It buys you room to decide what you actually want.
Look back at the list of decent things you wrote weeks ago. Add three more from the last few days.
You do not need to be finished or flawless to deserve kindness. You deserve it now, mid-way, as you are.
If a conversation turns belittling, you can end it politely. Something as simple as, I will leave it there for now, is enough.
Give a promise to yourself the same status as an appointment with someone else. Put it in your diary if that helps it feel real.
Your tone towards yourself on a bad day matters more than on a good one. Practise warmth exactly when it feels least deserved.
Consider which habits make you feel more like yourself and which leave you feeling smaller. Gently lean towards the first kind.
Respect includes looking after the ordinary basics: sleep, water, fresh air, a tidy corner. These are not trivial; they are foundations.
When you hear yourself say I always mess this up, try adding the word sometimes. Accuracy is often kinder than exaggeration.
Allow yourself to take up a little more space this week, physically or in conversation. Sit back, speak up, let the silence hold.
Choose one boundary you set earlier and check whether it has held. If it slipped, restate it without anger.
You can be someone who disappoints others occasionally and is still a good person. Both things are true for everyone.
Treat your own opinions as worth hearing. In your next meeting or chat, share one view you would normally keep to yourself.
Celebrate a promise kept, even quietly. A cup of tea, a deep breath, or a simple well done marks the moment.
Notice who in your life already treats you well. Spend a little more time in their company and let it recalibrate what feels normal.
Over the past two months you have practised dozens of small acts of self-respect. They add up to a different relationship with yourself.
Write down the kind of treatment you are no longer willing to accept. Keep it short and plain, and read it once a week.
Kindness to yourself might now feel slightly more natural than it did. Let that be enough without needing it to be constant.
When a setback comes, ask what you need rather than what you did wrong. The answer often points towards care.
Someone who respects themselves can still be humble, curious and wrong. Those qualities fit together perfectly well.
Think about how you would like to speak to yourself in five years. Practise one sentence in that voice right now.
Keep the promises that matter and gracefully renegotiate the rest. Being reliable to yourself does not require rigidity.
If you slip back into old habits for a day or a week, that is normal. Return to the smallest promise and begin again from there.
You are becoming someone who expects to be treated decently. Notice how that shows up in your posture, your voice and your choices.
Make a list of the promises to yourself that have become routine. They are no longer effort; they are simply part of who you are.
Self-respect is contagious in a quiet way. Others may begin to treat themselves better simply by watching how you behave.
Choose one longer-term commitment to yourself, such as a class, a weekly swim or a regular walk, and start it gently this week.
Look for one small way to honour your future self, such as laying out tomorrow's clothes or prepping a meal. It is a promise in action.
Respectful self-talk does not need to be cheerful. Calm, steady and fair is often the most supportive voice of all.
Reflect on a moment recently when you held your ground without drama. That steadiness is a skill you have built.
You may notice you tolerate less nonsense than you used to. That is not hardness; it is clarity.
Hold onto the phrase My needs count too. Bring it out whenever you feel yourself shrinking.
Being on your own side is not selfish. It makes you a more honest friend, partner and colleague.
Think back to the voice you heard in your head in the first week. How has it changed since then?
With only a week left, choose the three practices that helped you most. Write them somewhere you will find them again.
Respect is not a finish line. It is a way of living that you can return to every morning.
Your word to yourself has more weight now than it did. Protect that trust as you would any precious relationship.
You have learned that decency starts at home, in the way you think and speak about yourself. Keep that home warm.
As this stretch comes to an end, picture yourself walking into tomorrow with your shoulders back and your promises intact.
Tomorrow there will be no note from us, and that is all right. You know how to keep faith with yourself now.
Thank you for these ninety-odd days of quiet effort. You treated yourself with care, again and again, and that is what self-respect is made of. Go gently.
